# vespera! Macro

The `vespera!()` macro is the entry point for every Vespera application. It scans your route folder at compile time, builds an `axum::Router` with all discovered handlers, and optionally writes an OpenAPI 3.1 spec file.

## Full Parameter Reference

```rust
let app = vespera!(
    dir = "routes",                    // Route folder (default: "routes")
    openapi = "openapi.json",          // Output path (writes file at compile time)
    title = "My API",                  // OpenAPI info.title
    version = "1.0.0",                 // OpenAPI info.version (default: CARGO_PKG_VERSION)
    docs_url = "/docs",                // Swagger UI endpoint
    redoc_url = "/redoc",              // ReDoc endpoint
    spec_url = "/openapi.json",        // Raw OpenAPI JSON endpoint (application/json)
    servers = [                        // OpenAPI servers array
        { url = "https://api.example.com", description = "Production" },
        { url = "http://localhost:3000",   description = "Development" }
    ],
    security_schemes = [               // OpenAPI components.securitySchemes
        { name = "bearerAuth", type = "http", scheme = "bearer", bearer_format = "JWT" },
        { name = "apiKey", type = "apiKey", in = "header", header_name = "X-API-Key" }
    ],
    security = ["bearerAuth"],         // Optional document-level security
    tags = [                           // OpenAPI top-level tag descriptions
        { name = "users", description = "User operations" },
        { name = "admin", description = "Admin operations" }
    ],
    merge = [crate1::App1, crate2::App2]  // Merge child vespera apps
);
```

A relative `openapi` path resolves against the crate's `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR`, so a workspace member writes the file next to its own `Cargo.toml`.

## OpenAPI `info` and `servers`

- `title` and `version` fill `info.title` / `info.version` (defaults: `"API"` and the crate's `CARGO_PKG_VERSION`).
- `info.description` defaults to the crate's `description` from `Cargo.toml`.
- Without `servers = [...]` (or `VESPERA_SERVER_URL`) the document has **no** `servers` entry, so Swagger UI and generated clients call the origin that serves the spec.
- `tags = [...]` adds top-level tag descriptions for the tags your routes use.

## Security Schemes

Declare schemes with `security_schemes`, then attach requirements to routes with `#[vespera::route(security = [...])]`. Each entry becomes an OpenAPI security requirement with empty scopes; `security = []` on a route emits an explicitly unauthenticated operation. A route referencing an unknown scheme is a compile error (checked after `merge`).

```rust
let app = vespera!(
    openapi = "openapi.json",
    docs_url = "/docs",
    security_schemes = [
        { name = "bearerAuth", type = "http", scheme = "bearer", bearer_format = "JWT" },
        { name = "apiKey", type = "apiKey", in = "header", header_name = "X-API-Key" },
        { name = "basicAuth", type = "http", scheme = "basic" }
    ],
    security = ["bearerAuth"] // optional document-level default
);

#[vespera::route(get, path = "/me", security = ["bearerAuth"])]
pub async fn current_user(...) -> ... { ... }

#[vespera::route(get, path = "/health", security = [])]
pub async fn health() -> &'static str { "ok" }
```

Supported `type` values are OpenAPI's camelCase wire names: `"apiKey"`, `"http"`, `"mutualTLS"`, `"oauth2"` and `"openIdConnect"`. The DSL uses `header_name` for the api-key `name` field so it does not clash with the scheme's own `name`.

## Environment Variable Fallbacks

Every parameter has a corresponding environment variable. The macro parameter takes priority over the env var, which takes priority over the built-in default.

| Parameter | Environment Variable | Default |
|-----------|---------------------|---------|
| `dir` | `VESPERA_DIR` | `"routes"` |
| `openapi` | `VESPERA_OPENAPI` | none |
| `title` | `VESPERA_TITLE` | `"API"` |
| `version` | `VESPERA_VERSION` | `CARGO_PKG_VERSION` |
| `docs_url` | `VESPERA_DOCS_URL` | none |
| `redoc_url` | `VESPERA_REDOC_URL` | none |
| `spec_url` | `VESPERA_SPEC_URL` | none |
| `servers` | `VESPERA_SERVER_URL` + `VESPERA_SERVER_DESCRIPTION` | none |

## Documentation Endpoints

`docs_url`, `redoc_url` and `spec_url` each add an opt-in `GET` route. Every path must start with `/`, and no two of them may share a path — both mistakes are compile errors.

- **`docs_url`** serves Swagger UI and **`redoc_url`** serves ReDoc. Their assets load from unpkg at exact pinned versions with Subresource Integrity (`integrity` + `crossorigin="anonymous"`), so a tampered CDN file is refused by the browser. The spec is embedded in the page and escaped for the `<script>` context, so `</script>` or `<!--` inside a description or example cannot break the page.
- **`spec_url`** serves the generated OpenAPI document — including `merge`d apps — as `application/json`, ready for client generators and API gateways. The docs pages keep embedding the spec instead of fetching `spec_url`, so they still work when the router is nested under a prefix.

```rust
let app = vespera!(
    docs_url = "/docs",
    redoc_url = "/redoc",
    spec_url = "/openapi.json"
);
```

The pinned asset versions are `swagger-ui-dist` 5.34.0 and `redoc` 2.5.4; a page behind a Content Security Policy must allow those unpkg URLs. The renderers are public in `vespera::docs` if you want to serve a page yourself:

| Item | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `swagger_ui_html(spec_json: &str) -> String` | Swagger UI page with the spec embedded |
| `redoc_html(spec_json: &str) -> String` | ReDoc page with the spec embedded |
| `escape_json_for_script(json: &str) -> String` | Escapes `<`, `>`, `&`, U+2028 and U+2029 so JSON is safe inside `<script>` |
| `SWAGGER_UI_VERSION` / `REDOC_VERSION` | The pinned asset versions |

## Common Patterns

### Minimal — just a router

```rust
let app = vespera!();
```

### With Swagger UI

```rust
let app = vespera!(docs_url = "/docs");
```

### Write OpenAPI file + Swagger UI

```rust
let app = vespera!(
    openapi = "openapi.json",
    docs_url = "/docs",
    title = "My API",
    version = "1.0.0"
);
```

### Multiple OpenAPI output files

```rust
let app = vespera!(
    openapi = ["openapi.json", "docs/api-spec.json"]
);
```

### Custom route folder

```rust
// Scans src/api/ instead of src/routes/
let app = vespera!(dir = "api");
```

### With state and middleware

```rust
let app = vespera!(docs_url = "/docs")
    .with_state(AppState { db: pool })
    .layer(CorsLayer::permissive())
    .layer(TraceLayer::new_for_http());
```

### Merging child apps

```rust
let app = vespera!(
    openapi = "openapi.json",
    docs_url = "/docs",
    merge = [billing::BillingApp, notifications::NotificationsApp]
)
.with_state(app_state);
```

## The `.serve()` Extension

`vespera!()` returns an `axum::Router`. Vespera adds a `.serve(addr)` extension trait that replaces the usual `TcpListener::bind` + `axum::serve(...)` boilerplate:

```rust
use vespera::{vespera, Serve};

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    vespera!(docs_url = "/docs")
        .serve("0.0.0.0:3000")
        .await
}
```

`addr` accepts anything `tokio::net::ToSocketAddrs` takes — strings like `"0.0.0.0:3000"`, tuples like `("127.0.0.1", 8080)`, or a `SocketAddr`.

The router is served with `ConnectInfo<SocketAddr>`, so handlers can extract the peer address with `ConnectInfo(addr): ConnectInfo<SocketAddr>`.

`serve_with_graceful_shutdown(addr, signal)` stops accepting connections once `signal` resolves and returns after in-flight requests finish:

```rust
use vespera::{vespera, Serve};

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    vespera!(docs_url = "/docs")
        .serve_with_graceful_shutdown("0.0.0.0:3000", async {
            // requires tokio's `signal` feature
            let _ = tokio::signal::ctrl_c().await;
        })
        .await
}
```

## export_app! Macro

Export a Vespera app from a library crate so it can be merged into a parent app:

```rust
// In the child crate's src/lib.rs
mod routes;

// Scans "routes" folder by default
vespera::export_app!(MyApp);

// Or with a custom directory
vespera::export_app!(MyApp, dir = "api");
```

This generates a struct with two associated items:
- `MyApp::OPENAPI_SPEC: &'static str` — the OpenAPI JSON spec as a static string
- `MyApp::router() -> Router` — a function returning the Axum router

The parent app merges it with `merge = [MyApp]` in `vespera!()`.

# Route Attribute & Extractors `#[vespera::route]` marks a `pub async fn` as an HTTP handler. Vespera reads the function signature to extract path parameters, query parameters, request body, and response types for the OpenAPI spec. ## Route Attribute Parameters ```rust #[vespera::route( get, // HTTP method (default: get) path = "/{id}", // Path suffix (appended to file-based prefix) tags = ["users", "admin"], // OpenAPI tags description = "Get user by ID" // OpenAPI operation description )] pub async fn get_user(Path(id): Path) -> Json { ... } ``` | Parameter | Type | Default | Description | |-----------|------|---------|-------------| | method | `get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete`, `head`, `options` | `get` | HTTP method | | `path` | string | `""` | Path suffix appended to the file-based prefix | | `tags` | string array | `[]` | OpenAPI tags for grouping in Swagger UI | | `operation_id` | string | function name | OpenAPI `operationId`. Colliding default ids are module-qualified; two identical explicit ids are a compile error | | `summary` | string | first paragraph of the doc comment | OpenAPI operation summary | | `description` | string | doc comment after its first paragraph | OpenAPI operation description (the whole doc comment when `summary` is given). An explicit value disables doc-comment extraction | | `status` | `2xx` integer | `200` | Success status, e.g. `status = 204`; `204` / `304` document no body. A non-`2xx` value is a compile error | | `error_status` | integer array | none | Extra schema-less error statuses, e.g. `error_status = [404]` | | `responses` | `[(status, Type)]` | none | Typed error bodies, e.g. `responses = [(404, NotFoundError)]`; `Type` must implement `Schema` | | `security` | string array | document default | Security requirements, e.g. `security = ["bearerAuth"]`; `security = []` marks the operation unauthenticated | | `headers` | array of `{ name, required?, description? }` | none | Header parameters read by custom extractors; `required` defaults to `false` | | `request_example` | JSON string | none | Request body example; invalid JSON is emitted as a string value | | `response_example` | JSON string | none | `200` response example; invalid JSON is emitted as a string value | | `deprecated` | bare flag | off | Marks the operation `deprecated: true` (`#[deprecated]` on the handler does the same) | ```rust #[vespera::route( put, path = "/{id}", tags = ["users"], operation_id = "updateUser", summary = "Update a user", security = ["bearerAuth"], headers = [{ name = "X-Trace-Id" }], request_example = r#"{"name":"Alice"}"#, deprecated )] pub async fn update_user(...) -> ... { ... } ``` Without `summary` / `description`, the handler's doc comment is used: its first paragraph becomes the `summary`, the remaining paragraphs the `description`. ## Extractor to OpenAPI Mapping Vespera reads your handler's extractor types and maps them to OpenAPI parameters and request bodies automatically: Extractor OpenAPI Location Notes `Path` Path parameters `T` can be a primitive or a struct `Query` Query parameters Struct fields become individual query params `Json` Request body (`application/json`) `Form` Request body (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`) `TypedMultipart` Request body (`multipart/form-data`) Typed with schema `Multipart` Request body (`multipart/form-data`) Untyped, generic object `TypedHeader` Header parameters `State` Ignored Internal — not part of the API `Extension` Ignored Internal — not part of the API
## Examples ### Path Parameters ```rust // Single path param #[vespera::route(get, path = "/{id}")] pub async fn get_user(Path(id): Path) -> Json { ... } // Multiple path params via struct #[derive(Deserialize)] pub struct PostParams { pub user_id: u32, pub post_id: u32, } #[vespera::route(get, path = "/{user_id}/posts/{post_id}")] pub async fn get_post(Path(params): Path) -> Json { ... } ``` ### Query Parameters ```rust #[derive(Deserialize, Schema)] pub struct ListUsersQuery { pub page: Option, pub limit: Option, pub search: Option, } #[vespera::route(get)] pub async fn list_users(Query(q): Query) -> Json> { ... } ``` ### JSON Body ```rust #[derive(Deserialize, Schema)] pub struct CreateUserRequest { pub name: String, pub email: String, } #[vespera::route(post)] pub async fn create_user(Json(req): Json) -> Json { ... } ``` ### Validated Body (with 422) ```rust use vespera::Validated; use garde::Validate; #[derive(Deserialize, Schema, Validate)] pub struct CreateUserRequest { #[garde(length(min = 3, max = 32))] pub username: String, #[garde(email)] pub email: String, } #[vespera::route(post)] pub async fn create_user( Validated(Json(req)): Validated>, ) -> Json { ... } ``` ### State (Ignored by OpenAPI) ```rust #[vespera::route(get)] pub async fn list_users( State(db): State, // ignored by OpenAPI Query(q): Query, // included in OpenAPI ) -> Json> { ... } ``` ### Error Responses ```rust #[derive(Serialize, Schema)] pub struct ApiError { pub message: String, } #[vespera::route(get, path = "/{id}")] pub async fn get_user( Path(id): Path, ) -> Result, (StatusCode, Json)> { if id == 0 { return Err(( StatusCode::NOT_FOUND, Json(ApiError { message: "Not found".into() }), )); } Ok(Json(User { id, name: "Alice".into() })) } ``` A handler returning `Result<_, E>` documents a single inferred `400` error, because the macro cannot read the runtime `StatusCode`. Declare the real statuses with `responses` (typed bodies, a JSON `$ref` per status) and/or `error_status` (schema-less). As soon as any of them is present the explicit set is authoritative and the inferred `400` is dropped unless you list it; a typed `responses` entry wins over `error_status` for the same code. ```rust #[vespera::route(get, path = "/{id}", responses = [(404, ApiError)])] pub async fn get_user(...) -> Result, (StatusCode, Json)> { ... } // 204 success + 404 error — no 200, no 400 #[vespera::route(delete, path = "/{id}", status = 204, error_status = [404])] pub async fn delete_user(Path(id): Path) -> Result { ... } ``` ## Handler Requirements - Must be `pub async fn` — private or non-async functions are ignored - Must have `#[vespera::route]` attribute - Can live anywhere in `src/routes/` (or your configured `dir`) - The URL is: **file path prefix + `path` attribute value**

# API Reference

Complete reference for Vespera's macros and attributes.

## vespera! Macro

The entry point for every Vespera application. Scans your route folder at compile time, builds an `axum::Router`, and optionally writes an OpenAPI spec file.

See [vespera! Macro](/documentation/api/api-1) for the full parameter reference.

## Route Attribute & Extractors

`#[vespera::route]` marks a `pub async fn` as an HTTP handler. Vespera reads the function signature to extract path parameters, query parameters, request body, and response types for the OpenAPI spec.

See [Route Attribute & Extractors](/documentation/api/api-2) for all options and extractor mappings.

## schema_type!, schema!, and export_app!

- `schema_type!` — derive request/response DTOs from existing structs with `pick`, `omit`, `partial`, `add`, and SeaORM relation support
- `schema!` — get a `Schema` value at runtime with optional field filtering
- `export_app!` — export a Vespera app for merging into a parent app

See [schema_type! & More](/documentation/api/api-3) for the full reference.

# Schema & OpenAPI Generation Vespera generates a complete OpenAPI 3.1 spec from your Rust types at compile time. Derive `Schema` on any type used in a handler's input or output and it appears in the spec automatically. ## Deriving Schema ```rust #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, vespera::Schema)] pub struct User { pub id: u32, pub name: String, pub email: String, pub bio: Option, // optional — not in `required` array } ``` Vespera respects all standard serde attributes: ```rust #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, vespera::Schema)] #[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")] pub struct CreateUserRequest { pub user_name: String, // → "userName" in OpenAPI pub email: String, #[serde(rename = "fullName")] pub name: String, // → "fullName" in OpenAPI #[serde(skip)] pub internal_id: u64, // excluded from schema pub bio: Option, // optional field } ``` ## Custom serde Conversions Some serde attributes hand a value to your own code, so its wire shape is no longer the Rust type's. Document it with `#[schema(value_type = T)]`: ```rust #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, vespera::Schema)] pub struct Event { // `ts_seconds` writes an integer, not a date-time string. #[serde(with = "vespera::chrono::serde::ts_seconds")] #[schema(value_type = i64)] pub created_at: DateTime, // No value_type: documented as any value (`{}`) with a note. #[serde(with = "my_hex")] pub checksum: Vec, } #[derive(Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, vespera::Schema)] #[serde(into = "String", try_from = "String")] // documented as `string` pub struct Rgb { pub r: u8, pub g: u8, pub b: u8 } ``` Attribute Documented as Field `#[schema(value_type = T)]` `T`'s schema; other `#[schema(...)]` keys still apply Field `#[serde(with / serialize_with / deserialize_with)]` without `value_type` `{}` (any value) with a description. A one-sided key only affects its direction Container `#[serde(into = "T")]` `T` in responses; requests keep the fields (`{Name}Input`) Container `#[serde(from = "T")]` / `try_from` `T` in requests (`{Name}Input`); responses keep the fields Container `#[schema(value_type = T)]` `T` in both directions
An `Option` field read by a custom deserializer is `required` in request bodies, because serde no longer fills a missing field with `None`. ## Request Views (`{Name}Input`) serde can read a type differently than it writes it. When that happens, `Json` / `Form` / `TypedMultipart` request bodies reference an extra `{Name}Input` component, FastAPI-style, while responses keep using `{Name}`: ```rust #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, vespera::Schema)] pub struct Settings { pub theme: String, #[serde(default)] // optional in SettingsInput, required in Settings pub notifications: bool, #[serde(skip_deserializing)] // absent from SettingsInput pub updated_at: String, } ``` A type gets an input view when it has `#[serde(default)]` on a field or the container, one-sided `skip_deserializing` / `skip_serializing`, a `rename(deserialize = "..")` / `rename_all(deserialize = "..")` that differs from the serialize side, a container `from` / `try_from`, or a field whose type has its own input view. In `{Name}Input` defaulted fields are not `required`, `skip_deserializing` fields are absent and keys use the deserialize names. No `Input` component is emitted when both views are identical or no request body uses the type. `#[schema(name = "X")]` gives `XInput`; when a type already owns that name, the first free `XInput2`, `XInput3`, … is used. Types generated by `schema_type!` derive `Schema` too, so they follow the same rule. ## Type Mapping Rust Type OpenAPI Schema `String`, `&str` `string` `i8`–`i128`, `u8`–`u128` `integer` `f32`, `f64` `number` `bool` `boolean` `Vec` `array` with items `Option` T (parent marks field as optional) `HashMap` `object` with `additionalProperties` `BTreeSet`, `HashSet` `array` with `uniqueItems: true` `Uuid` `string` with `format: uuid` `Decimal` `string` with `format: decimal` `NaiveDate` `string` with `format: date` `NaiveTime` `string` with `format: time` `DateTime`, `DateTimeWithTimeZone` `string` with `format: date-time` `FieldData` `string` with `format: binary` `Ipv4Addr`, `Ipv6Addr` `string` with `format: ipv4` / `ipv6` `IpAddr`, `SocketAddr`, `PathBuf` `string` `url::Url` `string` with `format: uri` `serde_json::Value`, SeaORM `Json` / `JsonValue` `{}` (any JSON value) `()` empty response (204 No Content) Custom struct `$ref` to `components/schemas`
## Generic Types All type parameters must also derive `Schema`: ```rust #[derive(Schema)] struct Paginated { items: Vec, total: u32, page: u32, } ``` ## SeaORM Integration `schema_type!` has first-class support for SeaORM models. Relation fields are converted automatically: ```rust #[derive(Clone, Debug, DeriveEntityModel)] #[sea_orm(table_name = "memos")] pub struct Model { #[sea_orm(primary_key)] pub id: i32, pub title: String, pub user_id: i32, pub user: BelongsTo, // → Option> pub comments: HasMany, // → Vec pub created_at: DateTimeWithTimeZone, // → chrono::DateTime } vespera::schema_type!(Schema from Model, name = "MemoSchema"); ``` SeaORM Type Generated Schema Type `HasOne` `Box` or `Option>` `BelongsTo` `Option>` `HasMany` `Vec` `DateTimeWithTimeZone` `chrono::DateTime`
Circular references (e.g. User ↔ Memo) are detected automatically and handled by inlining fields to prevent infinite recursion. ## Database Defaults in OpenAPI Fields with SeaORM database defaults get `default` values in the generated schema: | SeaORM Attribute | OpenAPI Default | |-----------------|-----------------| | `primary_key` (Uuid) | `"00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000"` | | `primary_key` (i32/i64) | `0` | | `default_value = "NOW()"` | `"1970-01-01T00:00:00+00:00"` | | `default_value = "gen_random_uuid()"` | `"00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000"` | | `default_value = "true"` | `true` | > `required` is determined solely by nullability (`Option`). Fields with defaults are still `required` unless they are `Option`. ## Configuring the OpenAPI Output Pass parameters to `vespera!()` to control the spec: ```rust let app = vespera!( openapi = "openapi.json", // write spec to this file at compile time title = "My API", version = "1.0.0", docs_url = "/docs", // Swagger UI redoc_url = "/redoc", // ReDoc spec_url = "/openapi.json", // raw spec as application/json servers = [ { url = "https://api.example.com", description = "Production" }, { url = "http://localhost:3000", description = "Development" } ] ); ``` See [vespera! Macro](/documentation/api/api-1) for the full parameter reference.

# `Validated` and 422 `Validated` is a Vespera extractor wrapper that validates the extracted value **before** your handler is called. Invalid requests are rejected with `422 Unprocessable Entity` and a canonical JSON error envelope — no per-handler error mapping, no boilerplate. ## Basic Usage Declare constraints with `#[schema(...)]` on a `#[derive(Schema)]` type. The derive generates the validator itself — **no extra dependency** — and the same constraints are written into the OpenAPI schema (`minLength`, `pattern`, `format`, `minimum`, …): ```toml [dependencies] vespera = "0.6" ``` ```rust use serde::Deserialize; use vespera::{Schema, Validated, axum::Json}; #[derive(Deserialize, Schema)] pub struct CreateUser { #[schema(min_length = 3, max_length = 32, pattern = "^[a-z0-9_]+$")] pub username: String, #[schema(format = "email")] pub email: String, #[schema(minimum = 18, maximum = 120)] pub age: u8, } #[vespera::route(post, tags = ["users"])] pub async fn create_user( Validated(Json(req)): Validated>, ) -> Json<&'static str> { // `req` has already passed validation — no manual checks needed. Json("ok") } ``` Validation is part of the default `validation` feature. With `default-features = false`, re-enable it with `features = ["validation"]`. ## Supported `#[schema(...)]` Constraints Key OpenAPI Checked at runtime `min_length` / `max_length` `minLength` / `maxLength` Yes `pattern = "..."` `pattern` (regex is checked at compile time) Yes `format = "email"` / `"url"` / `"uri"` / `"ipv4"` / `"ipv6"` / `"ip"` `format` Yes `minimum` / `maximum` `minimum` / `maximum` Yes (inclusive) `min_items` / `max_items` `minItems` / `maxItems` Yes `dive` — Validates a nested `Schema` field (errors are prefixed, e.g. `address.city`) `exclusive_minimum` / `exclusive_maximum` / `multiple_of` / `unique_items` / `format = "uuid"` Emitted No (annotation only) `value_type = T` Replaces the schema with `T`'s (see Schema & OpenAPI → Custom serde Conversions) No
## 422 Response Envelope When validation fails, Vespera returns `HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity` with this JSON body: ```json { "errors": [ { "path": "username", "message": "length is lower than 3" }, { "path": "email", "message": "not a valid email" } ] } ``` The envelope is identical regardless of which extractor failed — your API clients only need to handle one error shape. ### Deserialization failures use the same envelope Input that is well-formed but does not deserialize into the target type — a wrong JSON type, a missing field, an unparsable query, form or path value — is also reported as `422` with this envelope, and `path` points at the offending field (for example `"age"` or `"tags[1]"`). Malformed JSON syntax (`400`), a missing or unsupported `Content-Type` (`415`) and body-limit errors keep axum's default rejection. ## Supported Extractors `Validated` works with every common Axum extractor: Extractor Validates `Validated>` JSON request body `Validated>` URL-encoded form body `Validated>` URL query parameters `Validated>` Path parameters
Every route with a `Validated` or `ValidatedWith` argument documents the `422` response in the OpenAPI spec, wherever the argument sits in the signature (for example after a plain `Path`). ### The payload must implement `garde::Validate` `#[derive(Schema)]` generates `garde::Validate` only for a struct with named fields and at least one runtime `#[schema(...)]` rule. A rule-less struct or an enum inside `Validated` fails to compile at the argument, with an error saying that the type cannot be validated by `Validated` / `ValidatedWith`. To fix it, add a rule, derive `garde::Validate` yourself, or take the plain extractor. ## Context-Aware Validation: `ValidatedWith` `ValidatedWith` works like `Validated`, but validates with a context `C` borrowed from the router state. Use it for garde rules declared with `#[garde(context(C))]`. The state provides the context through `vespera::ValidationContext`. A state of type `C` implements it automatically. App state can expose a field without cloning it per request: ```rust use std::sync::Arc; use vespera::{Schema, ValidatedWith, ValidationContext, axum::Json}; pub struct TagPolicy { pub required_prefix: String, } pub struct AppState { pub tag_policy: TagPolicy, } impl ValidationContext for Arc { fn validation_context(&self) -> &TagPolicy { &self.tag_policy } } #[derive(serde::Deserialize, Schema, garde::Validate)] #[garde(context(TagPolicy as policy))] pub struct TaggedPost { #[garde(custom(|tags: &Vec, policy: &TagPolicy| { if tags.iter().all(|t| t.starts_with(&policy.required_prefix)) { Ok(()) } else { Err(garde::Error::new("bad tag prefix")) } }))] pub tags: Vec, } #[vespera::route(post)] pub async fn create_post(post: ValidatedWith>) -> &'static str { let Json(_post) = post.into_inner(); "ok" } ``` `ValidatedWith` wraps the same extractors as `Validated` and answers the same `422` envelope. The spec documents the wrapped body or query parameters plus the `422` response. The context never appears in the spec. Its second field is private, so take the argument by name and use `into_inner()`, `get()` or `Deref`. ## JNI Hoisting Under JNI, the same `422` body is **hoisted** into the binary wire header as `"validation_errors": [...]`. Java decoders can read validation errors directly from the header without parsing the response body — no special-casing needed on the Java side. ```json { "v": 1, "status": 422, "headers": { "content-type": "application/json" }, "validation_errors": [ { "path": "username", "message": "length is lower than 3" } ] } ``` ## Alternative: Using `garde` Directly For rules `#[schema(...)]` does not cover (custom validators, validation contexts, `inner(...)` rules), derive [`garde`](https://docs.rs/garde)'s `Validate` yourself. `Validated` is built against **garde 0.23**, so add exactly that version: ```toml [dependencies] vespera = "0.6" garde = { version = "0.23", features = ["derive", "email", "url"] } ``` ```rust use garde::Validate; use serde::Deserialize; use vespera::Schema; #[derive(Deserialize, Schema, Validate)] pub struct UpdateProfile { #[garde(length(min = 1, max = 100))] pub display_name: String, #[garde(url)] pub website: Option, #[garde(length(min = 8))] pub password: String, #[garde(range(min = 0.0, max = 5.0))] pub rating: f64, #[garde(inner(length(min = 1)))] pub tags: Vec, } ``` Use one approach per type: runtime `#[schema(...)]` constraints and `#[derive(garde::Validate)]` on the same struct both implement `garde::Validate` and fail to compile (`E0119`). `#[garde(...)]` rules are not reflected in the OpenAPI document. See the [garde documentation](https://docs.rs/garde) for the full list of available constraints.

# Core Concepts

Vespera is built on three ideas: file-based routing, compile-time schema extraction, and automatic request validation.

## File-Based Routing

Your folder structure becomes your URL structure. Drop a `pub async fn` with `#[vespera::route]` anywhere in `src/routes/` and Vespera discovers it at compile time — no manual router registration.

```
src/routes/
├── mod.rs           → /
├── users.rs         → /users
├── posts.rs         → /posts
└── admin/
    ├── mod.rs       → /admin
    └── stats.rs     → /admin/stats
```

See [File-Based Routing](/documentation/concept/concept-1) for the full rules.

## Schema & OpenAPI Generation

Derive `Schema` on any Rust type and Vespera includes it in the generated OpenAPI 3.1 spec. Serde attributes (`rename_all`, `rename`, `skip`, `default`) are respected automatically.

```rust
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, vespera::Schema)]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
pub struct CreateUserRequest {
    pub user_name: String,   // → "userName" in OpenAPI
    pub email: String,
    pub bio: Option<String>, // optional field
}
```

See [Schema & OpenAPI](/documentation/concept/concept-2) for type mapping and SeaORM integration.

## `Validated<T>` and 422

Wrap any extractor in `Validated<T>` to run `garde` validation before the handler runs. Invalid requests are rejected with `422 Unprocessable Entity` and a canonical JSON error envelope — no per-handler error mapping needed.

```rust
#[vespera::route(post)]
pub async fn create_user(
    Validated(Json(req)): Validated<Json<CreateUser>>,
) -> Json<&'static str> {
    Json("ok")
}
```

See [Validated & 422](/documentation/concept/concept-3) for the full contract.

# Installation

Get Vespera running in your Axum project in under five minutes.

## 1. Add Dependencies

```toml
[dependencies]
vespera = "0.6"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
```

> Vespera re-exports `axum` — use `vespera::axum` in your code instead of depending on `axum` directly. This keeps the version in sync automatically.
>
> **MSRV:** Rust 1.88 (edition 2024).

## 2. Create Your First Route

Create the routes folder and add a handler:

```
src/
├── main.rs
└── routes/
    ├── mod.rs
    └── users.rs
```

**`src/routes/mod.rs`** — declare every route file as a module:

```rust
pub mod users;
```

**`src/routes/users.rs`**:

```rust
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use vespera::Schema;
use vespera::axum::{Json, extract::Path};

#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, Schema)]
pub struct User {
    pub id: u32,
    pub name: String,
}

/// Get user by ID
#[vespera::route(get, path = "/{id}", tags = ["users"])]
pub async fn get_user(Path(id): Path<u32>) -> Json<User> {
    Json(User { id, name: "Alice".into() })
}

/// Create a new user
#[vespera::route(post, tags = ["users"])]
pub async fn create_user(Json(user): Json<User>) -> Json<User> {
    Json(user)
}
```

## 3. Set Up `main.rs`

```rust
mod routes;

use vespera::{Serve, vespera};

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    println!("Swagger UI: http://localhost:3000/docs");
    vespera!(
        openapi = "openapi.json",
        title = "My API",
        docs_url = "/docs"
    )
    .serve("0.0.0.0:3000")
    .await
}
```

`.serve(addr)` is a Vespera extension trait on `axum::Router`. It replaces the usual `TcpListener::bind` + `axum::serve(...)` dance with a single chained call. `addr` accepts anything `tokio::net::ToSocketAddrs` takes — strings, tuples, or `SocketAddr`.

## 4. Run

```bash
cargo run
# Open http://localhost:3000/docs
```

Your Swagger UI is live. The `openapi.json` file is written to the project root at compile time.

## Adding State and Middleware

Chain standard Axum methods after `vespera!()`:

```rust
let app = vespera!(docs_url = "/docs")
    .with_state(AppState { db: pool })
    .layer(CorsLayer::permissive())
    .layer(TraceLayer::new_for_http());
```

## JNI / Java Integration

To embed Vespera inside a Java/Spring application, enable the `jni` feature:

```toml
[dependencies]
vespera = { version = "0.6", features = ["jni"] }
```

Then add two lines to your Rust lib:

```rust
pub fn create_app() -> vespera::axum::Router {
    vespera!(title = "My API")
}

vespera::jni_app!(create_app);
```

See the [JNI / Java Integration](/documentation/theme) section for the full setup guide.

## Cron Jobs

Enable the `cron` feature to schedule background tasks:

```toml
[dependencies]
vespera = { version = "0.6", features = ["cron"] }
```

See [Features](/documentation/features) for usage details.

# Migrating to 0.6 The 0.6 release (unreleased) is a hardening pass: OpenAPI output becomes more faithful to what serde actually serializes, `Validated` reports deserialization errors through the `422` envelope, and the in-process / JNI transport gets default resource limits. This page lists every change that can affect an existing 0.5 application. ## OpenAPI Output - **Untagged enums** emit `anyOf` (previously `oneOf`). - **Tuple / newtype structs, fixed-size arrays and tuples** get real `array` / inner schemas instead of a generic object. - **`skip_serializing` / `skip_serializing_if` fields** are no longer `required`. - **Tagged newtype variants**, variant-level `skip` / `other`, and `Arc` / `Rc` / `Cow` / `NonZero*` wrappers are supported. - **Plain tuple returns** (e.g. `(StatusCode, Json)`) and body-less `error_status` codes are documented. - **Colliding default `operationId`s** are module-qualified. Two explicit, identical `operation_id = "..."` values are now a compile error. - **Known `headers::*` `TypedHeader` parameters** use the real HTTP header name. - **`Path`** parameters are typed per field (serde names). **`Query`** drops `skip` / `skip_deserializing` fields, expands `flatten`, and array fields carry `style: form, explode: true`. - **Opaque and raw bodies:** `impl IntoResponse` / `Response` / `Redirect` responses are description-only; `Html` is `text/html`, `Sse` is `text/event-stream`, `Bytes` / `Vec` are `application/octet-stream`; `Option>` request bodies are `required: false`. - **Type mappings:** `serde_json::Value` is `{}`, `std::time::Duration` is `{secs, nanos}`; `IpAddr` / `SocketAddr` / `PathBuf` are `string`, `Ipv4Addr` / `Ipv6Addr` carry `format: ipv4` / `ipv6` and `url::Url` `format: uri` (previously a `Schema` assertion error); `{*rest}` wildcards are documented as `{rest}`. - **`Validated` / `ValidatedWith`:** a route whose `Validated<...>` argument follows a `Path` argument now documents its `422` response. `ValidatedWith` arguments now document their request body / query parameters and `422` (previously both were missing). A `Validated` payload without `garde::Validate` (a rule-less `Schema` struct or an enum) is reported with a dedicated compile error at the argument. - **Custom serde conversions:** a field with `#[serde(with / serialize_with / deserialize_with)]` is documented as any value (`{}`) with a note instead of its Rust type (add `#[schema(value_type = T)]` for the real shape); container `#[serde(into = "T")]` documents responses as `T` and `from` / `try_from` documents requests as `T`; an `Option` read by a custom deserializer is `required` in requests. SeaORM `Json` / `JsonValue` columns are `{}` (previously `type: object`), and `schema_type!` maps `JsonValue` to `serde_json::Value`. - **Serde attributes:** `flatten` on `Option` makes `T`'s fields optional; an enum's `rename_all` no longer renames struct-variant fields; `rename_all_fields` and `deny_unknown_fields` (`additionalProperties: false`) are supported. ## Served URLs and Build Output - **Explicit route paths are used verbatim.** `#[route(path = "/my_route")]` now serves `/my_route` (previously kebab-cased to `/my-route`). Only segments derived from file and module names are kebab-cased. Update clients, or write the path in kebab-case yourself. - **`openapi = "..."` output location:** a relative path resolves against the crate's `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR`, so workspace members write `openapi.json` next to their own `Cargo.toml`. The cache directory honours `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`. - **`Serve`:** `serve()` provides `ConnectInfo`, and the trait gained `serve_with_graceful_shutdown(addr, signal)` — custom implementors must add it. - **Cron:** jobs start once per process even if `create_app()` runs several times, and run on a dedicated `vespera-cron` thread when no Tokio runtime is present. ### New compile errors Code that previously compiled with a silently wrong spec now fails at compile time: - an unknown security scheme referenced by `security = [...]` (checked after `merge`), - a malformed `#[schema(...)]` attribute, - an internally tagged enum (`#[serde(tag = "...")]`) with a scalar newtype payload, - duplicate explicit `operation_id`s. ## OpenAPI Accuracy Changes These changes alter the generated document of an existing application without any code change: - **No default server.** `servers: [{ url: "http://localhost:3000" }]` is no longer emitted; without `servers = [...]` / `VESPERA_SERVER_URL` the document omits `servers`, so Swagger UI and clients call the origin that serves the spec. Add `servers = [{ url = "http://localhost:3000" }]` to keep the old output. - **Summary from doc comments.** The first paragraph of a handler's doc comment becomes the operation `summary`, the remaining paragraphs the `description` (previously the whole comment was the `description`). An explicit `summary = "..."` keeps the whole doc comment as the description; an explicit `description = "..."` disables doc-comment extraction. - **`info.description`** defaults to the crate's `description` in `Cargo.toml`. - **Renamed schemas** (`#[schema(name = "UserDto")]`) are referenced by their custom name instead of an inline `{ "type": "object" }`. - **Recursive generics** such as `Tree` (`struct Tree { children: Vec> }`) become components named after the instantiation — base name plus each type argument joined with `_` (`Tree_i32`, `Tree_Vec_User`). Non-recursive generics (`Page`) are still inlined. - **Unit and alias returns.** `Result<(), E>` and `()` document an empty `200` without `content`; `axum::response::Result` documents its `ErrorResponse`; `type ApiResult = Result, AppError>` aliases are expanded; an unresolvable return type is documented by description only. - **serde naming.** `rename_all` now applies serde's exact field and variant rules (variant `XMLParser` with `camelCase` is `xMLParser`), and `rename(serialize = "..", deserialize = "..")` uses the deserialize name for request-only contexts (query / path parameters). - **More annotations**: `#[deprecated]` handlers and fields emit `deprecated: true`, `skip_deserializing` fields `readOnly`, `skip_serializing` fields `writeOnly`; doc comments keep Markdown indentation; per-variant `#[serde(untagged)]` emits an `anyOf`. - **Request views (`{Name}Input`).** When serde reads a type differently than it writes it — `#[serde(default)]` on a field or the container, `skip_deserializing` or `skip_serializing` (not both), `rename(deserialize = "..")` / `rename_all(deserialize = "..")` differing from the serialize side, or a field whose type has its own input view — `Json` / `Form` / `TypedMultipart` request bodies now reference an extra `{Name}Input` component: defaulted fields are not `required`, `skip_deserializing` fields are absent, and keys use the deserialize name. The `{Name}` component (the response view) is unchanged. No `Input` component is emitted when the two views are identical or no request body uses the type. `#[schema(name = "X")]` gives `XInput`; when a type already owns that name the first free `XInput2`, `XInput3`, … is used. Generated clients will see new request types for these bodies. - **Query parameters** honour container `#[serde(default)]`, `Option>` (all optional) and destructured `Query(Filter { .. })` / `_` patterns. ### New compile errors (OpenAPI accuracy) - `#[route(responses = [(404, NotFound)])]` where `NotFound` does not implement `Schema` (previously a dangling `$ref`). - A `#[route]` handler inside an inline `mod name { .. }` block of a route file (it could never be mounted; move it to its own file). Route modules declared behind `#[cfg(...)]` that are compiled out, and `#[cfg]`-gated handlers, are now skipped instead of producing an unresolved path. ## `Validated` Deserialization Errors `Validated>`, `Validated>`, `Validated>` and `Validated>` now turn **deserialization failures** (wrong type, missing field, unparsable value) into `422 Unprocessable Entity` with the same `{"errors":[{"path","message"}]}` envelope as rule violations. Previously these returned axum's plain-text rejections (`422` / `400`). Malformed JSON syntax (`400`) and `415` content-type errors are unchanged. See [Validated & 422](/documentation/concept/concept-3). ## In-Process / JNI Limits `SYNC` and `DIRECT` dispatch now run on the **shared** multi-threaded Tokio runtime instead of a per-Java-thread runtime, so connection pools and spawned tasks work across requests. New defaults bound resource use: Limit Default On violation Spring property (`vespera.bridge.native.*`) Buffered request body 64 MiB `413` `max-request-bytes` Buffered response body 256 MiB `500` `max-buffered-response-bytes` `dispatchAsync` in-flight calls 4096 `503` `async-max-in-flight` Streamed request body unlimited `413` `max-streaming-request-bytes` Dispatch deadline (streaming: until the header is committed) disabled `504` `dispatch-timeout` Shared runtime blocking threads 512 work queues `max-blocking-threads`
Set a limit to `0` to disable it. Outside Spring, use the `vespera.limits.*` / `vespera.async.*` / `vespera.runtime.*` system properties, the matching `VESPERA_*` environment variables, or the Rust-side setters in `vespera::inprocess` (for example `set_max_request_bytes`). Streaming dispatch also changed: - `dispatchStreaming` / `dispatchFullStreaming` throw `IOException` when the response fails **after** body bytes were written (previously a synthetic `500` header after a partial body). - `dispatchStreaming` hoists `422` `validation_errors` into the wire header like the buffered modes. ## Java Bridge (`vespera-bridge`) 1. **Spring is a provided dependency.** The bridge no longer exports `spring-boot-starter-web` / `jackson-databind`; declare them in your app if you relied on them transitively. Spring Boot 3.5 and 4 are supported. 2. **`HEAD` keeps the real `Content-Length`** of the matching `GET` instead of `Content-Length: 0`. 3. **Native library extraction** is per-user, permission-checked and content-addressed (`vespera-native-/` under `vespera.native.dir` / `VESPERA_NATIVE_DIR` / `/vespera-`) and reused across restarts. 4. **Autoconfiguration** is an `@AutoConfiguration` that also requires Spring MVC and the servlet API on the classpath. 5. **The new `configure*` methods return `boolean`** (`false` when the native side already fixed the value). `configureStreaming(int, int)` keeps its `void` signature. 6. **Upgrade the JAR and the native library together.** A new bridge JAR paired with a cdylib built against an older `vespera` crate binds the `configure*0` JNI hooks to the wrong signatures — rebuild the Rust library whenever you upgrade `vespera-bridge`. 7. **The app-selection header is client-controlled and no longer forwarded.** Restrict reachable apps with `vespera.bridge.exposed-apps` (unlisted names get `404` without dispatch); Rust handlers no longer see `X-Vespera-App`. 8. **Header values use a Latin-1 byte mapping** in both directions, so non-ASCII response header values are no longer dropped. 9. **Consumed form bodies are rebuilt.** `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` bodies already read by Spring (`FormContentFilter`, `CsrfFilter`) are reconstructed from the request parameters. 10. **Forwarded path:** the servlet context path, a prefix servlet mapping and `;` path parameters (e.g. `;jsessionid`) are stripped. 11. **Request ids:** responses carry `X-Request-Id` by default (`vespera.bridge.request-id.enabled` / `.header`). 12. **Proxy-generated errors** are `text/plain` (like Rust's `error_wire`) instead of Spring error pages; the unknown-app `404` no longer echoes the app name. `ASYNC` responses get no `Range` handling. 13. **Oversized buffered responses answer `500`, not `413`.** `vespera.bridge.max-buffered-response-bytes` (default 64 MiB) is forwarded to the native buffered-response cap unless `vespera.bridge.native.max-buffered-response-bytes` (or its sysprop/env) sets it. 14. **CORS preflights reach Rust by default.** `vespera.bridge.cors=rust` routes `OPTIONS` preflights to the Rust router (configure a `tower_http` `CorsLayer` there); set `vespera.bridge.cors=spring` to keep Spring MVC's CORS handling. 15. **Proxy errors are generic.** Unexpected failures answer `vespera dispatch failed` (details in the WARN log with the request id); a missing native library answers `503`. 16. **Bounded app names.** `DispatchEvent.app()` and the `app` metric tag report `UNKNOWN` for client-selected app names not known to be registered. 17. **Version check.** `VesperaBridge.init` fails when the native library's `major.minor` differs from the bridge's; `-Dvespera.native.versionCheck=warn` or `off` relaxes it. ### Gradle Plugin - `publishPlugins` fails without Plugin Portal credentials. - `cargoBuild` is now a `CargoBuildTask` instead of an `Exec`; build scripts that configure it as `Exec` must be updated. - A missing `Cargo.lock` no longer fails the build; `extraNativeLibs` and `targets` add multi-platform jars. - A hyphenated `crateName` now works (new optional `packageName` / `libName`), `bridgeVersion` defaults to the matching bridge release, and `cargoSourceRoots` is ignored.

# What is Vespera? **FastAPI-like developer experience for Rust.** Zero-config OpenAPI 3.1 generation for Axum. ```rust // That's it. Swagger UI at /docs, OpenAPI at openapi.json let app = vespera!(openapi = "openapi.json", docs_url = "/docs"); ``` Vespera scans your `src/routes/` folder at compile time, extracts every `#[vespera::route]` handler and `#[derive(Schema)]` type, and assembles a complete OpenAPI 3.1 spec — no annotations to maintain, no runtime reflection, no hand-written JSON. ## Why Vespera? Feature Vespera Manual Approach Route registration Automatic (file-based) Manual `Router::new().route(...)` OpenAPI spec Generated at compile time Hand-written or runtime generation Schema extraction `#[derive(Schema)]` on Rust types Manual JSON Schema Request validation `Validated` extractor → auto `422` Manual checks in every handler Server startup `.serve("0.0.0.0:3000")` one-liner `TcpListener::bind` + `axum::serve` Swagger UI Built-in Separate setup Type safety Compile-time verified Runtime errors
## Headline Capabilities Capability How `#[derive(Schema)]` → OpenAPI 3.1 Rust types become JSON Schema at compile time, including serde renames, `Option`, `Vec`, SeaORM relations `Validated` extractor + auto-`422` Wraps `Json`/`Form`/`Query`/`Path` and runs `garde::Validate` before the handler — rejection is `422` with a canonical JSON envelope `schema_type! { ... }` Derive request/response DTOs from existing structs (`pick` / `omit` / `partial` / `add` / `multipart` / `omit_default`) with first-class SeaORM relation support One-liner `.serve(addr)` Extension trait on `axum::Router` — replaces `TcpListener::bind` + `axum::serve` boilerplate JNI / Spring integration Embed your Axum router inside a Java/Spring app in-process — no TCP, no base64, raw bytes end to end Cron jobs `#[vespera::cron("...")]` — auto-discovered like routes, runs via a built-in tokio scheduler
## JNI Performance Numbers When embedding Vespera inside a Java/Spring application via JNI, the `SmartDispatchModeResolver` (default since vespera-bridge 0.2.0) picks the cheapest safe path per request. Measured on a `GET /health` round-trip through the real JNI boundary (AMD Ryzen 9 9950X, Java 21, Windows 11): Request shape Mode ns / round-trip Small/bodyless + idempotent (GET/HEAD/PUT/DELETE/OPTIONS, ≤ 256 KiB) `DIRECT` (pooled direct buffers) ~2,200 ns Small (≤ 256 KiB) + non-idempotent (POST/PATCH) `SYNC` (heap-buffered) ~3,200 ns Large or unknown-length body `BIDIRECTIONAL_STREAMING` ~24,100 ns
Binary streaming throughput (64 MiB payload, bidirectional): Chunk size Throughput 16 KiB ~10,408 MiB/s 64 KiB ~11,587 MiB/s 256 KiB ~14,458 MiB/s
The `direct_pooled` path completes a tiny `/health` round-trip in **2,349 ns/op** — **1.55× faster** than the pre-0.2.0 sync baseline (3,643 ns/op). ## How It Works ``` src/routes/ ├── mod.rs → / ├── users.rs → /users └── admin/ └── stats.rs → /admin/stats ``` 1. You place `pub async fn` handlers in `src/routes/` and annotate them with `#[vespera::route]`. 2. The `vespera!()` macro scans the folder at compile time, discovers every handler, and builds an `axum::Router`. 3. Types annotated with `#[derive(Schema)]` are extracted into OpenAPI component schemas automatically. 4. The generated `openapi.json` and Swagger UI are served at the URLs you configure. ## Get Started Head to [Installation](/documentation/installation) to add Vespera to your project in under five minutes.

# Dispatch Modes & Wire Format ## Binary Wire Format Both request and response use the same length-prefixed layout: ``` bytes 0..4 : u32 BE = header_json byte length N bytes 4..4+N : UTF-8 JSON (request) { "v":1, "method", "path", "query"?, "headers"? } (response) { "v":1, "status", "headers", "metadata", "validation_errors"? } bytes 4+N.. : raw body bytes (UTF-8 text or binary — no encoding applied) ``` Key properties: - No base64 — multipart uploads, PDFs, and images travel as raw bytes - `"v":1` is the protocol version; mismatched versions return a `400` wire response - `"validation_errors"` is an optional array hoisted from `422` JSON bodies — Java decoders read validation errors from the header without parsing the body - All failure paths (malformed wire, Rust panic, no app registered) return a valid length-prefixed response, so the decoder never has to special-case errors ## Dispatch Modes `VesperaBridge` exposes seven native methods — all sharing the same wire format, the same registered router, and the same panic-safe `catch_unwind` discipline: Method Mode Java return Memory `dispatchBytes(byte[])` sync `byte[]` (header + body) full body in memory `dispatchAsync(CompletableFuture, byte[])` async `void` (future completes) full body in memory `dispatchStreaming(byte[], OutputStream)` sync, response-streaming `byte[]` (header only) chunk-bounded response `dispatchFullStreaming(byte[], InputStream, OutputStream)` sync, bidirectional streaming `byte[]` (header only) chunk-bounded both ways `dispatchStreamingWithHeader(byte[], Consumer, OutputStream)` sync, response-streaming `void` (header via callback) chunk-bounded response `dispatchFullStreamingWithHeader(byte[], Consumer, InputStream, OutputStream)` sync, bidirectional streaming `void` (header via callback) chunk-bounded both ways `dispatchDirect(ByteBuffer, int, ByteBuffer)` sync, direct buffers `int` (response length / overflow code) no Java heap arrays
### Choosing a Mode - Small JSON RPC, single request/response → `dispatchBytes` - Hot small/bounded payloads where JNI copy overhead matters → `dispatchDirect` / `dispatchDirectPooled` - Async I/O coordination (parallel Java requests, non-blocking) → `dispatchAsync` + `CompletableFuture` - Large download / streaming response (video, PDF, SSE) → `dispatchStreaming` + `OutputStream` - Large upload + large download (file transfer, video transcoding) → `dispatchFullStreaming` + `InputStream` + `OutputStream` - The `*WithHeader` variants let Spring-style controllers commit status/headers before the first body byte is written ## SmartDispatchModeResolver (Default since 0.2.0) The autoconfigured default since vespera-bridge 0.2.0 picks the cheapest safe path per request. Measured on a `GET /health` round-trip through the real JNI boundary: | Request shape | Mode | ns / round-trip | |---------------|------|-----------------| | Small/bodyless + idempotent (GET/HEAD/PUT/DELETE/OPTIONS, ≤ 256 KiB) | `DIRECT` | ~2,200 | | Small (≤ 256 KiB Content-Length) + non-idempotent (POST/PATCH) | `SYNC` | ~3,200 | | Large or unknown-length body | `BIDIRECTIONAL_STREAMING` | ~24,100 | Trade-offs: - **DIRECT** writes the wire response straight into a pooled per-thread direct `ByteBuffer` (64 KiB → `vespera.direct.maxBufferBytes`, default 4 MiB). Responses larger than the pooled buffer trigger a single retry that **re-runs the Rust handler** — which is why DIRECT is gated on idempotent methods only. - **SYNC** fully buffers the response on the JVM heap. The 256 KiB request-size gate keeps the response size reasonable for JSON-RPC-shaped traffic. - **BIDIRECTIONAL_STREAMING** is unchanged for large/unknown-length bodies — multi-GB upload + multi-GB download runs chunk-bounded, ~32 KiB resident each side. Restore the pre-0.2.0 default (every request that may carry a body streams both ways, ~24 µs uniform): ```yaml vespera: bridge: dispatch-mode: bidirectional-streaming ``` ## Direct Buffer Dispatch `dispatchDirect(ByteBuffer in, int inLen, ByteBuffer out)` eliminates the two JNI `GetByteArrayRegion`/`SetByteArrayRegion` copies that `dispatchBytes` pays. The response is streamed straight into the out buffer — no intermediate `Vec`. Measured at **1.4–3.4× per round-trip** versus `dispatchBytes` depending on payload size. Contract: - Both buffers MUST be direct (`ByteBuffer.allocateDirect`); heap buffers are rejected with `IllegalArgumentException` - The request is read from absolute offsets `in[0..inLen]` — the buffer's position/limit are ignored; `inLen` is authoritative - Return `>= 0`: a complete wire response occupies `out[0..n]` - Return `< 0`: `-(requiredSize)` — the response did not fit; **retrying re-runs the Rust handler**, so only retry idempotent requests - `Integer.MIN_VALUE`: response exceeds 2 GiB `dispatchDirectPooled(byte[] wireRequest, boolean retryOnOverflow)` wraps the raw call with per-thread reusable direct buffers (64 KiB initial, doubling up to `vespera.direct.maxBufferBytes`, default 4 MiB). ## Direct API (Without the Proxy Controller) ```java import com.devfive.vespera.bridge.VesperaBridge; import com.devfive.vespera.bridge.VesperaBridge.DecodedResponse; // 1. Initialise once at startup VesperaBridge.init("my_rust_lib"); // 2. Encode a request byte[] wireRequest = VesperaBridge.encodeRequest( "POST", "/documents/validate", /* query */ null, Map.of("content-type", "application/json"), "{\"title\":\"…\"}".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)); // 3. Dispatch through Rust byte[] wireResponse = VesperaBridge.dispatchBytes(wireRequest); // 4. Decode DecodedResponse resp = VesperaBridge.decodeResponse(wireResponse); System.out.println(resp.status()); // 200 System.out.println(resp.headers()); // { "content-type": "application/json", … } System.out.println(new String(resp.bodyBytes())); // copies the raw response body ``` > **0.2.0 breaking change:** `DecodedResponse.body()` now returns a read-only `java.nio.ByteBuffer` (zero-copy view over the wire bytes). The owned `byte[]` materialisation moved to `DecodedResponse.bodyBytes()`. Callers that previously used `body()` as `byte[]` must switch to `bodyBytes()`. ## Async Dispatch ```java CompletableFuture future = VesperaBridge.dispatch(wireRequest); future.thenAccept(wireResponse -> { DecodedResponse resp = VesperaBridge.decodeResponse(wireResponse); System.out.println("Status: " + resp.status()); }); ``` The future is **always** completed with a valid wire response, even on Rust panics or JNI conversion failures. You will never see a dangling future. ## Streaming Dispatch ```java byte[] wireRequest = VesperaBridge.encodeRequest( "GET", "/files/large.pdf", null, Map.of(), new byte[0]); try (ByteArrayOutputStream sink = new ByteArrayOutputStream()) { byte[] headerOnly = VesperaBridge.dispatchStreaming(wireRequest, sink); DecodedResponse meta = VesperaBridge.decodeResponse(headerOnly); System.out.println("Status: " + meta.status()); System.out.println("Body size: " + sink.size()); } ``` ## Bidirectional Streaming ```java try (InputStream upload = Files.newInputStream(Path.of("huge.mp4")); OutputStream download = Files.newOutputStream(Path.of("transcoded.mp4"))) { byte[] wireHeader = VesperaBridge.encodeRequestHeader( "POST", "/transcode", null, Map.of("content-type", "video/mp4")); byte[] respHeader = VesperaBridge.dispatchFullStreaming( wireHeader, upload, download); DecodedResponse meta = VesperaBridge.decodeResponse(respHeader); System.out.println("Status: " + meta.status()); } ``` A 1 GiB upload paired with a 1 GiB download runs in low-single-digit MiB resident memory on each side. Backpressure is enforced naturally — if Axum reads slowly, `InputStream.read()` blocks on the bounded channel.

# Streaming & Multi-App

## Streaming Tuning

Both streaming knobs are fixed for the process lifetime once the first dispatch runs. Configuration precedence (first hit wins):

1. **Programmatic setter** — `VesperaBridge.configureStreaming(chunkBytes, channelCapacity)` (call before or after `init`)
2. **System properties** — `vespera.streaming.chunkBytes`, `vespera.streaming.channelCapacity`
3. **Environment variables** — `VESPERA_STREAMING_CHUNK_BYTES`, `VESPERA_STREAMING_CHANNEL_CAPACITY`
4. **Built-in defaults** — 256 KiB chunk size, 16 channel slots

| Setting | System property | Env var | Default | Range |
|---------|----------------|---------|---------|-------|
| Chunk buffer size | `vespera.streaming.chunkBytes` | `VESPERA_STREAMING_CHUNK_BYTES` | 256 KiB | 4 KiB – 8 MiB |
| Request channel slots | `vespera.streaming.channelCapacity` | `VESPERA_STREAMING_CHANNEL_CAPACITY` | 16 | 1 – 1024 |
| Tokio worker threads | `vespera.runtime.workerThreads` | `VESPERA_RUNTIME_WORKERS` | logical CPUs | 1 – 1024 |

### Java API

Call before `VesperaBridge.init(...)` for guaranteed precedence:

```java
VesperaBridge.configureStreaming(
    131072,  // chunkBytes: 128 KiB (clamped to 4 KiB – 8 MiB)
    32       // channelCapacity: 32 slots (clamped to 1 – 1024)
);
VesperaBridge.init("my_rust_lib");
```

When called before `init()`, values are stored as pending and applied immediately after the native library loads — before any dispatch can occur. This ensures the programmatic setter beats system properties and environment variables.

Throws `IllegalArgumentException` if `chunkBytes` is outside `[4096, 8388608]` or `channelCapacity` is outside `[1, 1024]`.

### System Properties

```bash
java -Dvespera.streaming.chunkBytes=131072 \
     -Dvespera.streaming.channelCapacity=32 \
     -jar app.jar
```

### Environment Variables

```bash
export VESPERA_STREAMING_CHUNK_BYTES=131072
export VESPERA_STREAMING_CHANNEL_CAPACITY=32
java -jar app.jar
```

### Tuning Tips

- Larger chunks reduce the per-chunk JNI crossing cost (one `SetByteArrayRegion` + one `OutputStream.write` per chunk) at the price of per-stream memory. 256 KiB is a reasonable ceiling for throughput-oriented deployments.
- The Tokio worker-thread knob caps Rust's shared runtime — useful when the JVM's own pools (Tomcat request threads, virtual-thread carriers) compete with Tokio for the same cores, or when a container CPU limit is lower than the host's logical CPU count.

---

## Multi-App Routing

Multi-app routing is primarily a feature for external-dispatcher scenarios — JNI (Java host picks app per request via header), WebAssembly bridge, C FFI, or any in-process embedding where the host distinguishes between multiple independent Vespera API surfaces.

### Rust Side

```rust
pub fn create_app()  -> axum::Router { vespera!(title = "Default") }
pub fn admin_app()   -> axum::Router { vespera!(dir = "admin_routes",  title = "Admin") }
pub fn public_app()  -> axum::Router { vespera!(dir = "public_routes", title = "Public") }

vespera::jni_apps! {
    "_default" => create_app,
    "admin"    => admin_app,
    "public"   => public_app,
}
```

`jni_apps!` is the primary multi-app API. `jni_app!(create_app)` is syntactic sugar for a single default app.

### Java Side

The default `HeaderAppNameResolver` selects an app per request via the `X-Vespera-App` header:

```bash
# Default app (no header)
curl http://localhost:8080/health

# Admin app
curl -H "X-Vespera-App: admin" http://localhost:8080/dashboard

# Public app
curl -H "X-Vespera-App: public" http://localhost:8080/info
```

Each app's URLs are independent — the same `/users` path can mean different things in `admin` vs `public` apps. Unknown app names return `404`; invalid app names (special characters, > 64 bytes) return `400`.

> **Security:** the app-selection header is sent by the client. Any caller can ask for any registered app (for example `admin`) on a path your Spring Security rules treat as public. Restrict the reachable apps with `vespera.bridge.exposed-apps` (unlisted names get `404` without being dispatched), or replace `AppNameResolver` with one that derives the app from something the client cannot forge. The header itself is never forwarded to Rust.

### Custom App-Selection Strategy

```java
@Bean
public AppNameResolver myAppResolver() {
    // App name from the first path segment:
    //   /admin/dashboard  →  app "admin", path "/dashboard"
    //   /public/info      →  app "public", path "/info"
    return request -> {
        String uri = request.getRequestURI();
        if (uri.startsWith("/admin/")) return "admin";
        if (uri.startsWith("/public/")) return "public";
        return null;  // default app
    };
}
```

---

## Virtual Thread (Project Loom) Limitation

The pooled direct-buffer methods (`dispatchDirectPooled`) use `ThreadLocal<ByteBuffer[]>` to maintain per-thread reusable buffers. In Java 21+, `ThreadLocal` binds to the **virtual thread** (not the carrier thread) — so in a virtual-thread-per-request server, each virtual thread allocates a fresh direct buffer and loses all pooling benefit. Direct memory accumulates until the virtual thread is garbage-collected, potentially causing memory pressure under high concurrency.

**Recommendations for virtual-thread deployments:**

- Set `vespera.bridge.dispatch-mode=bidirectional-streaming` to opt out of the smart default, so `DIRECT` is never chosen by the autoconfigured resolver.
- Or use `dispatchBytes`, `dispatchStreaming`, or `dispatchFullStreaming` directly instead of the pooled direct variants.
- Or run dispatch on a bounded platform-thread executor (e.g. a `ForkJoinPool` with a fixed parallelism cap).
- Or lower `vespera.direct.maxBufferBytes` to reduce per-thread allocation size.

`DispatchMode.BIDIRECTIONAL_STREAMING` is safe for virtual threads and handles all payload sizes without pooling.

---

## 0.2.0 Breaking Changes

### 1. Default DispatchModeResolver Flipped to SmartDispatchModeResolver

Pre-0.2.0 the autoconfigured default was `BidirectionalStreamingDispatchModeResolver` — every request that may carry a body streamed both ways, ~24.1 µs per round-trip uniform. Since 0.2.0 the default is `SmartDispatchModeResolver`.

| Request shape | Pre-0.2.0 mode | 0.2.0+ mode |
|---------------|----------------|-------------|
| Small/bodyless idempotent (GET/HEAD/PUT/DELETE/OPTIONS, ≤ 256 KiB CL or no CL) | `STREAMING` / `BIDIRECTIONAL_STREAMING` | `DIRECT` |
| Small non-idempotent (POST/PATCH, ≤ 256 KiB CL) | `BIDIRECTIONAL_STREAMING` | `SYNC` |
| Large or unknown-length body | `BIDIRECTIONAL_STREAMING` | `BIDIRECTIONAL_STREAMING` |

Opt out (restore the pre-0.2.0 default):

```yaml
vespera:
  bridge:
    dispatch-mode: bidirectional-streaming
```

Or register a custom `DispatchModeResolver` bean — `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` ensures it wins over both the property and the autoconfigured default.

### 2. DecodedResponse.body() Returns ByteBuffer

`DecodedResponse.body()` now returns a read-only `java.nio.ByteBuffer` (zero-copy view over the wire bytes). The owned `byte[]` materialisation moved to `DecodedResponse.bodyBytes()`.

```java
// Before 0.2.0
byte[] body = resp.body();

// After 0.2.0
byte[] body = resp.bodyBytes();          // owned copy
ByteBuffer view = resp.body();           // zero-copy view
```

Callers that previously consumed `body()` as `byte[]` must switch to `bodyBytes()`.

---

## Migrating from the JSON-Envelope Bridge (≤ 0.0.13)

The pre-0.0.14 bridge used `dispatch(String) → String` with base64-encoded binary bodies.

| Before | After |
|--------|-------|
| `VesperaBridge.dispatch(json)` | `encodeRequest(...)` → `dispatchBytes(...)` → `decodeResponse(...)` |
| `body_bytes_b64` field on the response JSON | raw body bytes after the wire header (no base64) |
| ~33% size overhead on binary bodies | zero overhead |

Existing users of `VesperaProxyController` need no code change — the controller was rewritten to the new wire path internally. Direct callers of `VesperaBridge.dispatch(String)` must update; the old method was removed in 0.0.14.

# Spring Configuration

Every behaviour of the autoconfigured proxy can be tuned from `application.yml`. The JAR ships `META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json`, so IntelliJ IDEA and the Spring Tools for VS Code / Eclipse complete and document every `vespera.bridge.*` key (plus `management.health.vespera.enabled`) and offer the values of `dispatch-mode` and `cors`.

## Property Reference

```yaml
vespera:
  bridge:
    app-header: X-Vespera-App            # header the default AppNameResolver reads
    exposed-apps: [admin]                # apps that header may select (_default always)
    controller-enabled: true             # false = no proxy controller (BYO)
    include-patterns: ["/**"]            # paths the proxy serves
    exclude-patterns: []                 # paths left to Spring MVC
    dispatch-mode: smart                 # smart | bidirectional-streaming
    cors: rust                           # rust | spring
    direct-retry-on-overflow: true
    max-buffered-request-bytes: 67108864 # 64 MiB, 0 = unlimited
    max-buffered-response-bytes: 67108864 # 64 MiB, 0 = unlimited
    async-pool-size: 0                   # 0 = max(2, min(4, CPUs))
    clear-threadlocals-after-request: false
    request-id:
      enabled: true
      header: X-Request-Id
    library-name: my_rust_lib            # VesperaBridge.init(...) during startup
    shutdown-on-close: false
    shutdown-timeout: 10s
    native:                              # Rust-side knobs, see below
      max-request-bytes: 67108864
      max-streaming-request-bytes: 0
      max-buffered-response-bytes: 268435456
      dispatch-timeout: 30s
      async-max-in-flight: 4096
      worker-threads: 8
      max-blocking-threads: 512
```

| Property | Default | Effect |
|----------|---------|--------|
| `app-header` | `X-Vespera-App` | Header the default `HeaderAppNameResolver` reads to pick the app; absent → default app. Never forwarded to Rust |
| `exposed-apps` | empty | Apps the header may select. Any other name gets `404` without dispatch. While empty, any registered app is selectable and a one-time WARN is logged on the first non-default selection |
| `controller-enabled` | `true` | `false` disables `VesperaProxyController`; the `VesperaBridge` methods stay available |
| `include-patterns` | `["/**"]` | Spring `PathPattern`s the proxy serves |
| `exclude-patterns` | none | Patterns the proxy never serves, even inside `include-patterns` |
| `dispatch-mode` | `smart` | `smart` = `SmartDispatchModeResolver`; `bidirectional-streaming` restores the pre-0.2.0 default |
| `cors` | `rust` | Who answers CORS preflights and owns `Access-Control-*` headers |
| `direct-retry-on-overflow` | `true` | Only matters when a `DIRECT` overflow cannot use the native stash; `false` answers `500` instead of re-dispatching |
| `max-buffered-request-bytes` | 64 MiB | Request body cap for the buffered modes (`SYNC` / `ASYNC` / `DIRECT` / `STREAMING`) → `413`. Bidirectional streaming is exempt |
| `max-buffered-response-bytes` | 64 MiB | Response cap for `SYNC` / `ASYNC` → `500`. Forwarded to the native buffered-response cap unless that is set explicitly |
| `async-pool-size` | `0` | Threads of the executor that parses `ASYNC` responses; `0` keeps `max(2, min(4, CPUs))` |
| `clear-threadlocals-after-request` | `false` | `true` clears the per-thread direct/header buffers after every request (redeploy-heavy containers) |
| `request-id.enabled` / `.header` | `true` / `X-Request-Id` | Request-id propagation, see below |
| `library-name` | none | Crate name the autoconfiguration loads with `VesperaBridge.init(...)` when the application has not done it |
| `shutdown-on-close` / `shutdown-timeout` | `false` / `10s` | Stop the Rust runtime when the context closes, see below |
| `management.health.vespera.enabled` | `true` | Actuator health indicator |

## Proxied Paths

By default the proxy is a `/**` catch-all: more specific Spring MVC handlers (your `@RestController`s, `/error`, Actuator) still win, but everything else — including what Spring Boot would otherwise serve from `classpath:/static/` — goes to Rust. Narrow it with patterns matched against the path within the application (context path and a prefix `DispatcherServlet` mapping removed):

```yaml
vespera:
  bridge:
    include-patterns: ["/api/**", "/health"]
    exclude-patterns: ["/api/internal/**"]
```

A path outside `include-patterns`, or matching an `exclude-patterns` entry, is not mapped to the proxy at all: Spring MVC carries on with other controllers, static resources and finally its own `404`. With `cors: rust`, preflights for those paths are left to Spring too. An invalid pattern fails startup.

## App Selection

The app-selection header is sent by the client, so any caller can ask for any registered app on a path your Spring Security rules treat as public. List the apps clients may reach:

```yaml
vespera:
  bridge:
    exposed-apps: [admin, public]
```

Or replace `AppNameResolver` with a bean that derives the app from something the client cannot forge (see [Streaming & Multi-App](/documentation/theme/theme-3)). `DispatchEvent.app()`, the `app` metric tag and WARN logs report `UNKNOWN` for client-selected names not known to be registered, so random header values cannot create unbounded metric series.

## CORS

| `cors` | Preflights | `Access-Control-*` on responses |
|--------|-----------|----------------------------------|
| `rust` (default) | Routed to the Rust router — configure a `tower_http` `CorsLayer` there | A Rust header replaces one Spring or a filter already set |
| `spring` | Answered by Spring MVC (`addCorsMappings`, `@CrossOrigin`) or Spring Security `http.cors()` | A Rust header is dropped when Spring already set it |

With `rust`, do not also configure Spring CORS for proxied paths, and permit unauthenticated `OPTIONS` requests in Spring Security so preflights reach Rust.

## Native Limits, Timeouts and Runtime

`vespera.bridge.native.*` is forwarded to the `VesperaBridge.configure*` methods during context startup, before the proxy serves a request. A value that arrives after the first native dispatch is logged and ignored. Precedence for every knob (first hit wins, then fixed for the process): `vespera.bridge.native.*` / programmatic `configure*` → system property → environment variable → default.

| Spring property | System property / env var | Default | On violation |
|-----------------|---------------------------|---------|--------------|
| `max-request-bytes` | `vespera.limits.maxRequestBytes` / `VESPERA_MAX_REQUEST_BYTES` | 64 MiB | `413` |
| `max-streaming-request-bytes` | `vespera.limits.maxStreamingRequestBytes` / `VESPERA_MAX_STREAMING_REQUEST_BYTES` | unlimited | `413` |
| `max-buffered-response-bytes` | `vespera.limits.maxBufferedResponseBytes` / `VESPERA_MAX_BUFFERED_RESPONSE_BYTES` | 256 MiB | `500` |
| `dispatch-timeout` | `vespera.dispatch.timeoutMillis` / `VESPERA_DISPATCH_TIMEOUT_MS` | disabled | `504` |
| `async-max-in-flight` | `vespera.async.maxInFlight` / `VESPERA_ASYNC_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` | 4096 | `503` |
| `worker-threads` | `vespera.runtime.workerThreads` / `VESPERA_RUNTIME_WORKERS` | logical CPUs | — |
| `max-blocking-threads` | `vespera.runtime.maxBlockingThreads` / `VESPERA_RUNTIME_MAX_BLOCKING_THREADS` | 512 | work queues |

Set a limit to `0` to disable it. `dispatch-timeout` bounds the whole dispatch for `SYNC`, `ASYNC` and `DIRECT`; for the streaming modes it bounds only the time to the response header, so a long download that keeps making progress is never cut off.

Outside Spring, call the Java API before the first dispatch. Each method returns `false` (and logs a warning) when the native side already fixed the value:

```java
VesperaBridge.configureRuntime(8, 512);          // workers, max blocking threads
VesperaBridge.configureDispatchTimeout(30_000);  // milliseconds
VesperaBridge.configureAsyncMaxInFlight(4096);
VesperaBridge.init("my_rust_lib");
```

`configureLimits(...)` sets the body caps the same way, and `configureStreaming(chunkBytes, channelCapacity)` tunes streaming (see [Streaming & Multi-App](/documentation/theme/theme-3)).

## Request IDs

```yaml
vespera.bridge.request-id:
  enabled: true          # default
  header: X-Request-Id   # default
```

An incoming id (1–128 visible ASCII characters) is reused, otherwise a random UUID is generated. It is forwarded to Rust in the same header, echoed on the response (unless the Rust response sets it), put in the SLF4J MDC as `requestId` during dispatch, and included in WARN logs and `DispatchEvent`s.

## Health, Metrics and Errors

- **Health:** with Spring Boot Actuator on the classpath the `vespera` health indicator reports `UP` once the native library is loaded, `DOWN` before that and `OUT_OF_SERVICE` after `VesperaBridge.shutdown(...)`; details carry `bridgeVersion` and `nativeVersion`. Disable it with `management.health.vespera.enabled=false`.
- **Metrics:** register `DispatchObserver` beans to receive a `DispatchEvent(app, mode, method, path, status, durationNanos, panicked, requestId)` per request. With Micrometer and a `MeterRegistry` bean, a timer `vespera.bridge.dispatch` tagged `app`, `mode`, `status` and `outcome` (`SUCCESS`, `CLIENT_ERROR`, `SERVER_ERROR`, `PANIC`, …) is autoconfigured.
- **Panics:** a Rust panic answers `500` with `"panicked":"true"` in the wire metadata and is logged at WARN together with every other `5xx`.
- **Proxy errors** are `text/plain` (the same shape as Rust's `error_wire`). Unexpected failures answer the fixed body `vespera dispatch failed`, with the details only in the WARN log; a native library that was never loaded answers `503`.

## Shutdown and Redeploys

```yaml
vespera.bridge:
  library-name: my_rust_lib
  shutdown-on-close: true
  shutdown-timeout: 10s
```

`VesperaBridge.shutdown(Duration)` stops the shared Tokio runtime once: new dispatches answer `503` at once, in-flight dispatches of every mode are drained for up to the timeout, a pending `ASYNC` dispatch completes with `503`, and cron jobs stop. It cannot be undone in the same process. `shutdown-on-close` only acts when the autoconfiguration loaded the library itself through `library-name`; a library you initialised yourself is never shut down by Spring.

A JVM loads a native library through one class loader only and never unloads it, so a redeployed web app cannot load it again. On servlet containers that redeploy or host several apps, put `vespera-bridge` and the library in the container's shared lib (e.g. Tomcat `$CATALINA_BASE/lib`) or run one deployment per JVM.

## Native Library Loading

`VesperaBridge.init("crateName")` first looks for `native/{os}-{arch}/{libname}` on the classpath and extracts it content-addressed to `<dir>/vespera-native-<sha256-prefix>/`, then falls back to `System.loadLibrary`.

| Setting | Default | Effect |
|---------|---------|--------|
| `-Dvespera.native.dir` / `VESPERA_NATIVE_DIR` | `<java.io.tmpdir>/vespera-<user.name>` | Extraction directory (use an exec-permitted, persistent directory when `/tmp` is `noexec`). Must be owned by the current user and not writable by others, otherwise a private temp directory is used |
| `-Dvespera.native.libc=musl\|glibc` | detected from `/proc/self/maps` | On a musl (Alpine) JVM `native/linux-{arch}-musl/` is tried first; the glibc library is only a fallback with a WARN |
| `-Dvespera.native.versionCheck=warn\|off` | fail | `init` fails when the native library's `major.minor` differs from the bridge's |
| `-Dvespera.native.cleanupLegacy=false` | `true` | Keep the `vespera-<random>` copies older bridges left in `java.io.tmpdir` |
| `-Dvespera.direct.maxBufferBytes` | 4 MiB | Cap of the per-thread pooled `DIRECT` buffers |

Build a musl library with a `*-linux-musl` Rust target (a cdylib needs `RUSTFLAGS="-C target-feature=-crt-static"`); the Gradle plugin bundles such targets under `native/linux-{arch}-musl/`. Upgrade the bridge JAR and the native library together — both must come from the same release.
